When asked whether the current support for visually impaired students in Hong Kong is sufficient, Mr Cheng said he was satisfied, but pointed out that different types of visually impaired individuals have different needs, and therefore hoped that society could further achieve inclusion. In addition, Mr Cheng shared his 'tips' for achieving top marks, which lay in handwritten notes that help deepen memory, complemented by AI-assisted learning.

Mr Cheng shared that he will stay in Hong Kong to study politics and law at the University of Hong Kong, saying that his exposure to and encounters with the law over the years had sparked his interest in the field. He 'believes the law can bring equality and opportunity,' and therefore hopes to become a barrister in the future, using the law to advocate for legal accessibility for members of the public who lack financial means or are in poorer physical condition.

When asked about his thoughts on the current political instability in Hong Kong, Mr Cheng said his 'original intention remains unchanged,' believing that social and economic instability 'will not affect my original intention to pursue [law],' and that he 'believes the law can bring opportunities to people.' As for whether AI will replace legal work, Mr Cheng said that law requires an understanding of 'human nature and worldly affairs,' and that AI cannot replace human emotions.

On the path of growing up, the support of family members is of paramount importance. Mr Cheng's father said, 'He (Mr Cheng) is a very hardworking person,' believing that Mr Cheng's efforts and the message he conveys can 'encourage fellow travellers.' Cheng's father said, 'All parents hope their children grow up healthy.' Upon learning that Mr Cheng had an eye condition, it took him a long time to come to terms with reality, but fortunately they received assistance through organisations such as Ebenezer School.
